props.title: The Barkleys of Broadway
props.initialSlug: Astaire & Rogers reunite in Broadway battle of egos

sections.content: The final pairing of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers came a decade after their RKO glory days, marking their only color film together. The Barkleys of Broadway reunited Hollywood's most celebrated dance duo at MGM, stepping in after Judy Garland dropped out. The film cleverly mirrors their own partnership - depicting a successful husband-wife theatrical team whose relationship strains when the wife pursues serious dramatic roles. Like The Band Wagon (1953) and Easter Parade (1948), it showcases MGM's peak musical production values while offering meta-commentary on show business partnerships.

sections.content: The film's most memorable sequence has Rogers performing "They Can't Take That Away from Me" - a poignant callback to their rendition in Shall We Dance (1937), but this time as a dramatic ballad rather than a dance number. Director Charles Walters, who had just helmed Easter Parade (1948), brings polish and intimacy to the couple's interactions. The script by Betty Comden and Adolph Green cleverly plays with the duo's personas while delivering classic musical comedy situations.

While not reaching the innovative heights of their 1930s RKO collaborations like Flying Down to Rio (1933) or Roberta (1935), The Barkleys offers a mature reflection on long-term creative partnerships. Oscar Levant provides sharp comic relief as their pianist friend, continuing MGM's tradition of strong supporting characters seen in films like An American in Paris (1951). sections.content: The film marked not just the end of Astaire and Rogers as a team, but symbolized the transition from the elegant Art Deco musicals of the 1930s to MGM's more integrated story musicals of the 1950s. While films like Singin' in the Rain (1952) and The Band Wagon (1953) would perfect this new style, The Barkleys serves as a bridge between eras, maintaining the sophistication of their earlier work while embracing Technicolor spectacle.
